name: french yogurt cake
instructions:
Ratio 3:2:1:1 (flour:sugar:yogurt:oil) where 1 part = 1/2 cup. Standard 3-egg build:

Dry:
- 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour (not wheat or cake)
- 1 cup sugar
- 2 tsp baking powder (standard; range: 1-3 tsp is fine; I tend to do 1.5 — see notes)
- 1/2 tsp table salt

Wet:
- 3 eggs
- 1/2 cup plain yogurt
- 1/2 cup oil (vegetable or olive)
- Zest of 1-2 lemons
- 1 tsp vanilla

Bake at 350°F.

BUTTER CAN INTERLEAVE for either the yogurt or oil slot if you're out — same amount, no other changes. Butter added melted is NOT a leavener, so it doesn't require a baking powder adjustment (previous notes here said otherwise; walked back).

Optional / welcome additions: almonds or walnuts folded in (see notes — this cake carries nuts well); cinnamon, garam masala, or nutmeg. Note: lemon JUICE is a failure — zest only.

See notes for the SCALING TABLE (1 egg / 2 eggs / 3 eggs) — the 1-egg version is especially good for this recipe (see character note below for why).
notes:
=== THE CAKE'S CHARACTER — TEA CAKE, DRIER + BREADIER (READ THIS FIRST) ===

This cake is DRIER and BREADIER than [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]]. It reads more like a TEA CAKE than a proper dessert cake — less flavorful, sturdier crumb. That character has real disadvantages and real advantages, and understanding both is how you use the recipe well.

DISADVANTAGE: it's less flavorful than most cakes, and it dries out fast if fridged. Don't refrigerate for 2-3 days like you would a softer moister cake — this one turns dry and unappealing. Best eaten day-of or within 24 hours at room temp.

ADVANTAGES:
1. LESS FLAVORFUL BASE = NUTS STAND OUT. You can load this cake up with almonds and walnuts and their flavor actually shows. In a more flavorful cake the nuts get buried; here they're the character.
2. SMALL BATCHES WORK — 1-EGG VERSION IS OPTIMAL. Because the cake doesn't store well, making it small is often the right move. See SCALING TABLE for the 1-egg / 2-egg / 3-egg proportions.
3. EPHEMERAL TOPPINGS PAIR WELL. Compote, icing, powdered sugar, whipped cream — all work on this cake precisely because you should intend to eat it in one sitting anyway. Topping and cake share the same freshness constraint. See EPHEMERAL TOPPINGS note.
4. USES UP PLAIN YOGURT. Plain yogurt is otherwise hard to place — it's rarely called for in savory cooking, and greek yogurt has taken over its slot in most modern dessert recipes. This cake is a real home for plain yogurt when you have some to use.

CONTRAST WITH THE FRIDGE-FRIENDLY CAKES: [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]] and cornbread-style cakes are more flavorful AND store better in the fridge. Those cakes want larger batches with ROBUST TOPPINGS (ganache, american buttercream) that hold up over several days of fridged storage. This cake is the opposite: small, tea-cake, ephemeral, plain-yogurt-based. Different tools for different jobs.

=== 1 CUP FAT TOTAL — LOAD-BEARING RATIO ===

The 3:2:1:1 flour:sugar:yogurt:oil ratio hits 1 cup of fat total (1/2 cup yogurt + 1/2 cup oil). That's the anchoring math for the recipe.

BUTTER INTERLEAVE: butter can swap in for either the yogurt or oil slot if you're short — same 1/2 cup, no leavening adjustment needed (see baking powder note). It's not a distinct 'butter variant' — just a substitution when you're missing an ingredient.

=== PLAIN YOGURT ONLY — GREEK YOGURT DOESN'T WORK (NOT JUST 'PREFERRED') ===

Plain yogurt is not just preferred here — GREEK YOGURT DOESN'T WORK as a straight swap. Greek is strained (thicker, higher protein, lower water) and a direct plain-for-greek swap gives you a weird, spongy cake — the protein-water balance is wrong for this recipe.

To make greek yogurt work, you'd need to take an egg OUT (to rebalance protein), then adjust dry ingredients to compensate — at which point you're basically at [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]], which IS the recipe for greek yogurt. Two different cakes; use the right one for your yogurt.

Marked greek yogurt as clashing here.

=== BAKING POWDER RANGE — 1.5 TO 2.5 TSP (DOESN'T MAKE MUCH DIFFERENCE) ===

1.5 tsp is the current pick. Range is 1.5-2.5 tsp depending on how fluffy you want the cake — the low end reads slightly denser and more tea-cake-like, the high end reads slightly fluffier. Doesn't make much difference in practice.

BUTTER (MELTED) IS NOT A LEAVENER: earlier notes here said to cut baking powder to 1.5 tsp when using butter. Walked back — melted butter doesn't contribute leavening the way creamed butter does, so there's no reason to adjust baking powder when butter interleaves for yogurt or oil.

=== EPHEMERAL TOPPINGS — COMPOTE, ICING, POWDERED SUGAR, WHIPPED CREAM, PASTRY CREAM ===

Ephemeral toppings are the RIGHT direction for this cake. All of these work:
- FRUIT COMPOTE (strawberry, blueberry — make and serve immediately)
- ICING (simple powdered-sugar-and-water or powdered-sugar-and-lemon-juice)
- POWDERED SUGAR dusted on top
- WHIPPED CREAM alongside
- [[pastry-cream]] (crème pâtissière) — thick vanilla custard spread on top, especially good with sliced fresh fruit arranged over it. Best within 2-3 days of making; matches this cake's freshness constraint.

The common thread: all of these want to be eaten same-day or within a few days. Which is exactly what you should do with this cake anyway (it dries out if fridged) — so the toppings' freshness constraint aligns with the cake's.

WHY NOT ROBUST TOPPINGS LIKE BUTTERCREAM OR GANACHE: those toppings are designed to last several days in the fridge. Pairing them with this cake wastes their durability (the cake goes stale before the topping does). Save robust toppings for [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]] or cornbread-style cakes that actually store well fridged.

=== ALMONDS AND WALNUTS WELCOME — LOAD UP ===

Both almonds and walnuts work in the batter. Because the cake's base flavor is muted (see CHARACTER note), the nuts stand out more here than in most cakes — you can add generously (a full handful of each, or a lot of one) and they contribute both flavor and structural ballast.

=== SPICES WELCOME — CINNAMON, GARAM MASALA, NUTMEG ===

Cinnamon and garam masala both add a lot to this cake. Nutmeg also welcome. Earlier notes called nutmeg clashing — walked back, that claim was unjustified.

=== FAILURE — LEMON JUICE IN THE CAKE OR FROSTING ===

Lemon JUICE (not zest) is a failure in the batter (adds water and a sour acidity that doesn't land here). Zest is fine and encouraged. Same rule as elsewhere in the cookbook — when a recipe wants 'lemon,' it usually wants zest.

=== SCALING TABLE — 1 EGG / 2 EGGS / 3 EGGS (PLAIN VERSION) ===

| Ingredient | 1 egg (× 1/3) | 2 eggs (× 2/3) | 3 eggs (standard) |
|---|---|---|---|
| AP flour | 1/2 cup | 1 cup | 1 1/2 cups |
| Sugar | 1/3 cup | 2/3 cup | 1 cup |
| Plain yogurt | scant 3 tbsp | 1/3 cup | 1/2 cup |
| Oil | scant 3 tbsp | 1/3 cup | 1/2 cup |
| Eggs | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| Lemon zest | zest of 1 lemon | zest of 1-2 lemons | zest of 1-2 lemons |
| Baking powder | 2/3 tsp | 1 1/3 tsp | 2 tsp |
| Salt | pinch | 1/3 tsp | 1/2 tsp |
| Vanilla | 1/3 tsp | 2/3 tsp | 1 tsp |
| Total fat | ~1/3 cup | ~2/3 cup | 1 cup |

Pan sizes (approximate — 1-egg and 2-egg untested):
- 1 egg: 6-inch round or small loaf pan. Bake ~25-30 min at 350°F.
- 2 eggs: 8-inch round or standard loaf pan. Bake ~35-40 min at 350°F.
- 3 eggs: 9-inch round or 8x8 square. Bake ~45 min at 350°F.

1-egg is the optimal scale for this cake — small batch, eat in one sitting, no fridge storage needed.

=== STRAWBERRY JAM EXPERIMENT (MAY 9 2026) — DIDN'T WORK, GENERAL BAKING LESSON ===

Tried two changes at once: (1) reduced sugar slightly and folded strawberry jam into the batter; (2) moved almonds out of the batter and onto the top of the frosting.

Results — bad:
- Cake came out WAY sweeter than intended despite the sugar reduction. Probable cause: jam is ~50-60% sugar by weight even without corn syrup, so ~1/3-1/2 cup of jam carries 30-60g of added sugar — substantially more than a 'slight sugar reduction' offsets. Jam also concentrates sweetness perception via low water activity and pectin gel; grams read sweeter in baked form.
- Cake was FLUFFIER than normal — a mix of good and bad. Jam is ~30-40% water; folding it in dilutes the batter and suppresses gluten formation. Removing the almonds removed real structural ballast (almond flour, fat, protein).
- Net: more moisture + less ballast = a softer crumb that dissolves faster on the palate, which makes the sugar hit harder. Got a tummy ache after a few bites.

Lessons for next attempt:
1. Keep almonds IN the batter — they provide real structural ballast this cake depends on.
2. For strawberry flavor without the sugar load: use freeze-dried strawberry powder or unsweetened strawberry purée. Let the flavor knob and the sugar knob tune separately.
3. For intentional tenderness, sub ~1/3 of the AP with cake flour (reduces gluten without adding water).
4. Read jam labels: subtract grams-of-sugar-per-spoonful from the cake's sugar quantity 1:1.

=== CHOCOLATE VARIANT EXPERIMENT (AUG 13 2026) — DIDN'T WORK, GENERAL BAKING LESSON ===

Skipped the lemon zest and swapped 1/4 cup of flour for 1/4 cup of NATURAL cocoa powder.

Result — didn't turn out well:
- Fruity/funky flavor. Attribute to using NATURAL cocoa powder instead of CACAO POWDER or DUTCHED cocoa. Natural cocoa is more acidic and funky-fruity; dutched (or cacao) is smoother and more chocolate-forward.
- Spongey and flat texture. This texture works for the lemon version (that's part of the tea-cake character) but chocolate cakes should be fluffier and less tangy.

General baking lesson: the french yogurt cake base is tuned for a lemon-forward or plain register. Turning it into a chocolate cake needs more than a flour-for-cocoa swap — the tangy-and-spongey character that suits lemon fights chocolate. If retrying the chocolate direction:
- Use CACAO or DUTCHED cocoa, not natural.
- Probably needs recipe-level adjustments beyond the flour swap to hit the fluffier-less-tangy chocolate cake register (different fat ratio, adjusted baking powder/soda balance, maybe milk instead of yogurt).
why_i_like_this_recipe: Best pantry cake — nothing unusual like cocoa powder, cake flour, or espresso. Uses up plain yogurt (otherwise hard to place). The muted base means nuts stand out, so it takes well to being loaded with almonds and walnuts. Small-batch friendly (1-egg is optimal) and pairs cleanly with ephemeral toppings — compote, icing, powdered sugar, whipped cream — since it's meant to be eaten same-day rather than fridged anyway.
